entry: Norwegian playwright, regarded as the father of modern [[Drama|drama]]. He established himself as a theater director in Norway during the 1850s and won international recognition with the poetic plays *Brand* and *Peer Gynt* in the 1860s. From 1864 he lived for 27 years in Italy and Germany, mainly in [[Rome]], [[Dresden]] and [[Munich]], before moving to Christiania (now [[Oslo]]) in 1891. He pioneered theatrical realism and, after *Peer Gynt*, abandoned verse for realistic prose. Several of his later dramas were considered scandalous in an era when European theater was expected to uphold strict morals of family life. Critics often rate *The Wild Duck* and *Rosmersholm* as his best works, while he regarded *Emperor and Galilean* as his masterpiece. [[Sigmund Freud]] placed him on a par with Shakespeare and [[Sophocles]], and [[George Bernard Shaw]] argued that he had surpassed Shakespeare as the world's pre-eminent dramatist.

English experimental and theoretical chemist and physicist. He is noted for his discovery of [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]], which he termed "inflammable air." In an 1766 paper, *On Factitious Airs*, he described the density of this gas, which formed water on combustion. [[Antoine Lavoisier]] later reproduced the experiment and gave the element its name. Reclusive and publishing few papers, Cavendish conducted research notable for its accuracy and precision. His work included the composition of the atmosphere, the properties of different gases, the synthesis of water, the law governing electrical attraction and repulsion, and a mechanical theory of heat. His experiment to measure the density of the [[Earth]], which informs the calculation of the [[Gravitational constant|gravitational constant]], is known as the Cavendish experiment. He entered the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1748 but left without a degree, and in 1773 he was elected a trustee of the [[British Museum]].

American naturalist, essayist, poet and philosopher, and a leading transcendentalist. He is best known for *Walden*, a reflection on simple living in natural surroundings, and for "Civil Disobedience," originally published as "Resistance to Civil Government," which argues for citizen disobedience against an unjust state. His writings on natural history anticipated the methods and findings of ecology and environmental history, two sources of modern [[Environmentalism|environmentalism]]. A lifelong abolitionist, he lectured against the fugitive slave law and defended [[John Brown (abolitionist)|John Brown]]. His philosophy of civil disobedience later influenced [[Leo Tolstoy]], [[Mahatma Gandhi]] and [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] Born in Concord, Massachusetts, he was the son of a [[Pencil|pencil]] maker.

Swiss humanitarian and co-founder of the Red Cross. Born in [[Geneva]], he had business interests in French [[Algeria]] before 1859, when, on his way to petition [[Napoleon III]], he witnessed the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino in northern Italy. Horrified by the wounded soldiers' lack of care, he organized local people to aid them, and his book *A Memory of Solferino* advocated relief for the wounded without discrimination. In February 1863 he was a member of the five-person committee that founded what became the International Committee of the Red Cross, and in 1864 he took part in the diplomatic conference that led to the First Geneva Convention. A business scandal in 1867 brought bankruptcy and expulsion from the committee, and he spent decades in poverty and obscurity. A journalist rediscovered him in 1895, and in 1901 he shared the first Nobel Peace Prize with French pacifist Frédéric Passy. He had earlier founded the Geneva chapter of the [[YMCA]], and he died in the Swiss village of Heiden.

American actor known for an everyman image, whose career spanned five decades on Broadway and in Hollywood. Born and raised in Nebraska, he made his Hollywood film debut in 1935. He was nominated for the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Actor for *The Grapes of Wrath* (1940), and he starred in Westerns directed by [[John Ford]]. He also appeared in [[Alfred Hitchcock]]'s *The Wrong Man*. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *On Golden Pond* (1981), his final film role. He was the patriarch of an acting family that included his daughter [[Jane Fonda]].

American mobster associated with the Lucchese crime family of [[New York City]] from 1955 until 1980, when he was arrested on narcotics charges and became an FBI informant. His testimony resulted in fifty convictions, including that of caporegime Paul Vario. Hill entered the Witness Protection Program, but was removed from it in 1987. His life story was told in Nicholas Pileggi's book *Wiseguy* (1985) and in the film *GoodFellas* (1990), directed by [[Martin Scorsese]], in which Ray Liotta played him.

King of England (r. 1216–1272) and son of [[John, King of England|King John]]. He succeeded at the age of nine during the First Barons' War and later promised to abide by a later version of [[Magna Carta]]. After a revolt in 1232 he ruled personally, investing heavily in a handful of favorite palaces and castles. He adopted [[Edward the Confessor]] as his patron saint and rebuilt [[Westminster Abbey]]. Expensive foreign policies and unpopular officials led barons to seize power in 1258, creating the Provisions of Oxford. He was defeated and captured at the Battle of Lewes in 1264, but his son Edward later freed him. His reign of 56 years was the longest in medieval English history.

King of England (r. 1154–1189) and the first Plantagenet monarch. He ruled England, parts of Wales and Ireland, and much of France, including Normandy, Anjou and Aquitaine, an area later called the Angevin Empire. He was the grandson of [[Henry I of England|Henry I]], and his marriage to [[Eleanor of Aquitaine]] brought him control of Aquitaine. He restored royal administration in England, and his legal reforms laid the basis for English common law. His conflict with Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, over control of the English Church ended in Becket's murder in 1170. His sons rebelled in 1173 with support from their mother and several European states, but the revolt was defeated. In 1189 his son Richard and Philip II of France defeated him, and he died soon afterwards.

Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1084–1105) and a Salian ruler. In 1062 Archbishop Anno II of [[Cologne]] kidnapped him and governed in his place until he came of age in 1065. He clashed with the papacy over the [[Investiture Controversy]], the question of who could appoint bishops and abbots. After German bishops declared Gregory's election invalid, Pope [[Pope Gregory VII|Gregory VII]] excommunicated him in 1076. Henry sought absolution through his penitential Walk to Canossa in 1077, but the dispute continued. He later supported the antipope Clement III, who crowned him emperor in Rome in 1084. His younger son, Henry V, forced his abdication in 1105, and Henry died without absolution. His role in the Investiture Controversy and the Walk to Canossa ensured a profoundly contested legacy.

King of England (r. 1399–1413), also known as Henry Bolingbroke. He was the son of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, and the first monarch of the House of Lancaster. After being exiled, he rallied Lancastrian supporters, imprisoned Richard II and formally deposed him, usurping the throne. He was the first English ruler since the [[Norman Conquest]] whose mother tongue was English. Rebellions marked his reign, most seriously those of Owain Glyndŵr and of Henry Percy (Hotspur), who was killed at the Battle of Shrewsbury in 1403. His deposition of Richard II later contributed to the dynastic disputes of the [[Wars of the Roses]]. He was succeeded by his son, Henry V.

King of France (r. 1589–1610) and the first [[House of Bourbon|Bourbon]] monarch of France. Raised as a [[Huguenots|Huguenot]], he led Protestant forces in the [[French Wars of Religion]] and inherited the French throne from his distant cousin Henry III in 1589. He initially kept the Protestant faith and fought the Catholic League, which refused to accept a Protestant monarch. After four years of military stalemate he converted to Catholicism, reportedly saying that "Paris is well worth a Mass." His Edict of Nantes (1598) guaranteed religious liberties to Protestants, effectively ending the Wars of Religion. He reformed state finance, promoted agriculture and education, and built roads, bridges and canals. He began the first successful French colonization of the Americas. A Catholic zealot assassinated him in Paris, and he was succeeded by his son [[Louis XIII]].

King of England (r. 1100–1135), known as Henry Beauclerc. The fourth son of [[William the Conqueror]], he seized the English throne after William Rufus died in a hunting accident. He defeated his elder brother Robert at Tinchebray in 1106 and took control of [[Normandy]]. He strengthened royal government with the exchequer and itinerant justices, and many of his administrators were men of obscure background who rose through the ranks. His son William drowned in the White Ship disaster of 1120. Henry declared his daughter Matilda his heir, but on his death his nephew Stephen of Blois succeeded him, starting a period of civil war known as the Anarchy.

American-born British author and critic, regarded as a key transitional figure between literary realism and modernism. He was born in [[Manhattan]], the son of theologian Henry James Sr. and the brother of philosopher [[William James]]. Much of his life was spent in Europe, and he became a British citizen in 1915. His novels, such as *The Portrait of a Lady* (1881), explore the social and marital interplay between American émigrés, the English and continental Europeans. His later works, including *The Golden Bowl* (1904), are often described as Impressionist. His novella *The Turn of the Screw* (1898) has a reputation as the most analyzed and ambiguous ghost story in English. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1911, 1912 and 1916. [[Jorge Luis Borges]] wrote that he knew "of no stranger work than that of Henry James."

American diplomat and political scientist. A member of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]], he served as national security adviser from 1969 to 1975 and as secretary of state from 1973 to 1977, under [[Richard Nixon]] and [[Gerald Ford]]. He pursued détente with the [[Soviet Union]], opened relations with China and negotiated the Paris Peace Accords that ended American involvement in the [[Vietnam War]]. He was awarded the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize, which proved controversial. His shuttle diplomacy helped end the [[Yom Kippur War]]. Critics have accused him of war crimes over civilian deaths caused by policies including the bombing of Cambodia.

English sculptor and draftsman, best known for semi-abstract monumental [[Bronze|bronze]] sculptures placed in public settings around the world. His forms are usually abstractions of the human figure, typically mother-and-child or reclining figures, and many interpreters liken his reclining figures to the landscape of his native [[Yorkshire]]. He was instrumental in introducing [[Modernism|modernism]] to the United Kingdom. He also drew a series of Londoners sheltering from the [[The Blitz|Blitz]] during [[World War II]]. Although his large commissions made him very wealthy, he lived frugally, and most of his money went toward endowing the Henry Moore Foundation, which supports education and the arts.

English composer and organist of the middle Baroque era, generally considered one of the greatest English composers. He was extremely prolific, and his works include more than 100 songs, the tragic opera *Dido and Aeneas* and incidental music to *The Fairy Queen*, a version of Shakespeare's *A Midsummer Night's Dream*. His style is uniquely English, though it incorporates Italian and French elements. After a childhood as a chorister in the Chapel Royal, he was appointed copyist at [[Westminster Abbey]] in 1676. His earliest identifiable work is an [[Ode|ode]] for the King's birthday, written in 1670 when he was eleven. He wrote several anthems for the extraordinary bass voice of John Gostling, and between 1680 and 1688 he wrote music for seven plays.

King of England (r. 1509–1547) and the second Tudor monarch. He is known for his six marriages, his break with the [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic Church]] and his establishment of the [[Church of England]]. Henry sought an annulment of his marriage to [[Catherine of Aragon]] to secure a male heir. When Pope Clement VII refused, Archbishop [[Thomas Cranmer]] declared the marriage void in 1533. Henry passed the Acts of Supremacy, making himself Supreme Head of the Church of England, and dissolved the Catholic monasteries, seizing their wealth. He ordered the beheadings of two of his wives, Anne Boleyn and Catherine Howard. In later life he was morbidly obese and immobile. He was succeeded by his only surviving son, [[Edward VI]], and his daughters [[Mary I]] and [[Elizabeth I]] also ruled.

King of England (r. 1485–1509) and the first monarch of the [[House of Tudor|Tudor]] dynasty. He spent 14 years in exile in [[Brittany]] before his forces defeated Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field. He strengthened his claim by marrying Elizabeth of York. He was the last English king to win his throne on the battlefield, and he defended it at Stoke Field, which decisively ended the [[Wars of the Roses]]. He restored power and stability to the monarchy, raised new revenues through several new taxes, and paid close attention to detail. He was peacefully succeeded by his son, [[Henry VIII]].

King of England (r. 1422–1461; 1470–1471) and claimant to the French throne. He became king at the age of nine months and is the only English monarch to have been crowned king of France, at [[Notre-Dame de Paris]] in 1431. His reign saw the near-total loss of English lands in [[France]], and by 1453 Calais was the only English-governed territory on the continent. A mental breakdown that year triggered a power struggle that led to the [[Wars of the Roses]]. He was deposed by [[Edward IV]] in 1461 and briefly restored in 1470. He was possibly killed in the [[Tower of London]] on Edward's orders. He founded [[Eton College]] and King's College, Cambridge.

King of England (r. 1413–1422) and a warrior-king celebrated in [[William Shakespeare|Shakespeare]]'s Henriad. His victory at the [[Battle of Agincourt]] in 1415 and his conquest of Normandy gave England the upper hand in the [[Hundred Years' War]]. The Treaty of Troyes in 1420 recognized him as heir and regent of France, the high-water mark of the English cause in that war. At home he restored public order, worked closely with Parliament, and enforced strict religious orthodoxy by crushing the Lollard movement. He helped end the Western Schism at the Council of Constance. He died of [[Dysentery|dysentery]] seven weeks before the ailing Charles VI of France and was succeeded by his infant son, Henry VI. Modern assessments differ: some criticize his military ambition for bankrupting the realm, while others rank him among England's greatest kings.

American poet and educator, one of the Fireside Poets of [[New England]]. He was born in [[Portland, Maine]], taught at Bowdoin College and then at Harvard College, and retired from teaching in 1854 to devote himself to writing. His original works include the poems "Paul Revere's Ride," *The Song of Hiawatha* and *Evangeline*. He was the first American to translate [[Dante Alighieri|Dante]]'s *Divine Comedy* completely. For the rest of his life he lived in the Revolutionary War headquarters of [[George Washington]] in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]]. He became the most popular American poet of his day and enjoyed success overseas. After his death his poetry declined in popularity and came to be criticized as too sentimental and too derivative of European poetic styles.

Polish epic writer, known for historical novels set in the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]]. Born into an impoverished Polish noble family in the Kingdom of Poland, then part of the [[Russian Empire]], he began publishing journalistic and literary pieces in the late 1860s. In the late 1870s he traveled to the [[United States]], sending back travel essays that won him popularity with Polish readers. His Trilogy, comprising *With Fire and Sword*, *The Deluge* and *Sir Michael*, is set in the 17th-century Commonwealth. His international best seller *Quo Vadis* is set in [[Nero|Nero's]] [[Rome]]. He received the 1905 [[Nobel Prize]] in Literature for his "outstanding merits as an epic writer."

Style of Japanese pornographic [[Anime|anime]] and [[Manga|manga]], also found in artwork and video games. The Japanese word means *perversion* or *abnormality*, and in Japan it does not define a genre; such works are usually called *ero anime*, *ero manga* or *seijin manga* (adult manga). The Oxford Dictionary defines hentai in English as a subgenre of manga and anime characterized by overtly sexualized characters and sexually explicit images and plots. Many works are self-published and form a significant part of the market for doujin works.

[[Inflammation|Inflammation]] of the [[Liver|liver]] tissue, which may cause [[Jaundice|jaundice]], fatigue or no symptoms at all. Hepatitis is acute if it resolves within six months and chronic if it lasts longer. Chronic hepatitis may progress to [[Cirrhosis|cirrhosis]], liver failure or liver cancer. It is most commonly caused by the viruses hepatitis A, B, [[Hepatitis C|C]], D and E, while other causes include heavy alcohol use, certain medications, toxins and autoimmune disease. Hepatitis A and E spread mainly through contaminated food and water, and hepatitis B is mainly sexually transmitted. Hepatitis A, B and D can be prevented by immunization, and medications can treat chronic viral hepatitis. Worldwide in 2015, chronic hepatitis B affected about 343 million people and chronic hepatitis C about 142 million. Hepatitis results in more than a million deaths a year.

Infectious disease caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV), a type of viral [[Hepatitis|hepatitis]]. The virus persists in the [[Liver|liver]] and becomes chronic in about 70% of those infected, often causing liver disease over many years. It is spread mainly by blood contact, including injection drug use and [[Blood transfusion|transfusions]]. There is no vaccine, but antiviral medications cure more than 95% of chronic infections. In 2019 an estimated 58 million people worldwide were infected, and about 290,000 died from the virus, mainly from liver cancer and [[Cirrhosis|cirrhosis]].
